units.translation: The use of the personal pronouns ἐγώ [I] and σύ [you] in dialogue, in which two or more persons converse about their own affairs, is far more frequent than in anapaests and lyric songs. Moreover, the pronouns ἐγώ [I] and σύ [you], as I noted in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 135, since the first and second persons of the verb are inherent in them, can either be added to the verb or omitted. They are omitted where there is no reason for the person to be indicated more explicitly, but they are added where one person is contrasted with another, which very often happens through the particles μέν – δέ [on the one hand – on the other hand], and not rarely at the beginning of a sentence or where the person for whatever reason is to be indicated more explicitly. Although the dramatic poets did not follow these rules so diligently that they did not often add pronouns for the sake of metrical convenience where they could have omitted them, or omit them where they would have been suitably added, nevertheless in such places too they used sound and subtle judgment and always had a fitting reason for adding or omitting the pronoun.
The examples of the pronoun in Aeschylus, arranged according to the order of cases, are these:
By crasis ἐγώ [I] coalesces with ἅ [which] into ἁγώ [I who] Suppl. 980. More frequently ἐγώ [I] and the other cases in κἀγώ [and I], κἀμοῦ [and of me], κἀμέ [and me]: see under the word καί [and].
ἐγώ [I] undergoes aphaeresis after οἴ [alas], οι'γώ [I alas] Sept. 808. Pers. 517. Ch. 691, 887, 893, 928.
The enclitic dative μοι [to me] coalesces with ἐστί [is] into μοὐστί [is to me] Ch. 122.

The situation of the other cases is almost the same, which themselves too are found very often in dialogue, rarely in anapaests, which are often between dialogues, and even more rarely in lyric songs.
